title: Correlated subqueries
description: A correlated subquery references a column from the OUTER query, so it re-runs once per outer row instead of just once. Write a query that returns the `first_name` and `salary` of every employee who earns more than the average salary of their own department.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: correlated subquery

The inner AVG(salary) needs to look at only THAT employee's department - so the subquery must filter its own employees rows by comparing department_id to the outer query's current row, e.g. e2.department_id = e.department_id.
Alias employees twice (e and e2): outer WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id).
expected_behavior: Returns first_name and salary for employees earning above their own department's average salary.
solution: SELECT e.first_name, e.salary FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id);
explanation: Unlike the plain subquery in the previous exercise (computed once, up front), a correlated subquery depends on the outer row and conceptually re-runs for each one - powerful, but worth knowing it can be slower on large tables than an equivalent JOIN/window function.
